video_title: The People Who’ve Survived Collapse | with Victoria Sweet | TGS 243
transcript: >> If we go to the original environmental  movements, a lot of the tenets are,   we have to keep humans out of it. We  have to have these protected areas. But   when you talk to indigenous peoples, that's  completely different. Humans are a part of   the environment. Without humans doing their job,  stewarding the lands, stewarding the plants and   the animals in a positive way, you're not  going to have as thriving of a community. >> Today I'm pleased to be joined by my friend  Victoria Sweet, who is the founder of the Ishkode   Fund. Uh, today we will explore how indigenous  ideas can help address our hardest challenges,   and how Victoria, uh, enables critical  funding to reach indigenous-led groups.   Uh, Victoria Sweet is an immediate descendant of   the White Earth Nation and granddaughter  of a native boarding school survivor. Through the Ishkode Fund, Victoria works to  restore balance between people and the Earth,   as well as provide support that will help  strengthen the fire of indigenous leadership   and innovation that has long sustained native  communities. She has worked at the National   Council of Juvenile and Family Court Judges,  where she trained state and tribal judges hearing   domestic violence and human trafficking  cases involving native community members. She also worked with the Whitener Group  supporting tribal justice systems in Alaska, and   as the director of the di- indigenous communities  portfolio of grantees during her time at the NoVo   Foundation. In our conversation, Victoria explains  that donating to indigenous-led causes is not a   matter of charity, but instead an investment and  reciprocal relationship from which we all benefit. She shares specific examples of  how indigenous communities share   knowledge that benefits everyone nearby, despite  indigenous-led organizations receiving only one   quarter of 1% of philanthropic dollars in the  United States. Beyond philanthropy, though,   uh, Victoria challenges each of us  to get to know a local indigenous   community and be open to the possibility  of learning something new and unexpected. With that, please welcome Victoria Sweet. Victoria Sweet, great to see you.  Welcome to The Great Simplification. >> Thanks, Nate. >> So you are the founder and CEO of the  Ishkode Foundation, and you are of direct   ancestry with the White Earth Nation, which  I believe is Ojibwe. And you've spent most of   your career strengthening systems to protect  indigenous people, including justice reform,   tribal court development, um, and  now community-led philanthropy. Uh, maybe you could start by saying  what the word Ishkode means and why   that was central to your work and your,  your trajectory that brought you here. >> Thanks. Yes. The Ishkode is actually a word in  the Anishinaabe language, and a lot of indigenous   languages are not noun-based languages, so  they don't translate exactly into English. So at-- the simplest form, Ishkode  means fire, but it's more than just   fire. It's fire as medicine. It's fire  as transformation. It's the fire that   exists in every single person when you feel  something inside of you, like a spark, an idea,   a knowing about something. And in our tradition,  a name is so much more than just a name. It's an idea that guides sort of the  path that your life is meant to walk.   So when this fund was originated, it made a lot  of sense to me that we needed to name it first   because that gave it some direction, some  guidance. How can we take a fund that's all   about flowing money and turn it into some kind  of healing fire, some kind of transformation? And then when you have this  transformative fire and you   look at the world with the fires  that are burning down and all of   the damage and destruction that has been  done, you have unhealthy, harmful fire,   and then you have its opposite. And I'd really  love to see this fund represent the opposite. >> So I wanna get to your fund, um, in  a moment and the work that you're doing. But two, uh, um, pre-questions. What do you  think the role of philanthropy is generally   in the meta-crisis world and facing all the  things that we're facing? And then a subset of   that is my understanding is a very tiny percent  of philanthropy is directed towards indigenous,   uh, populations, and you're  trying to increase that. So maybe you could set the, the stage for  that. Um, why is this work so important now? >> Philanthropy can play a very interesting  role. Uh, it's philanthropic d- um,   donated charitable dollars. So oftentimes  you can use philanthropy for things that   investments and other types of capital  won't do. It can seed fund something   where an investor says, "Well, we have to  have certain, uh, guarantees to back it." A philanthropist doesn't have to do that. So it  can be a part, an essential part of a capital   stack. Philanthropy can go in and buoy up. So for  instance, we fund a lot of nonprofits. For me,   a nonprofit organization is an organization that  fills in gaps. What is the government not doing   effectively? What does, what do the people  in the community say, "We need more of this,   and we don't think it's going to  happen through these other ways. We're going to start our own nonprofits." A lot  of philanthropic dollars go to those nonprofits   as gap fillers for areas that the community  recognizes we need more support. And you know,   I think a lot of people don't  understand the power of what it   means to fund indigenous communities. I  think there's a lot of misunderstandings. I think there's a lot of prejudices. I think  there's a lot of people who only see the   negative in our communities. And because of that,  they think, "Well, we actually have the answers,   and then we'll help these native peoples,  these indigenous peoples." And they haven't   had a chance to actually see the beauty  of what these communities have to offer. And because of that, they continue to go and fund  other things, fund in other ways, and are missing   an incredible opportunity, which is a group  of people, communities all over the world,   who have knowledge that has existed long before  the modern structures that we're living in today. >> What are the statistics in the  United States, North America, the world? Like, what, what percent of people, what is the  population of what you might label indigenous? >> It depends on how you define us.  You'll, you'll see it anywhere from,   like, 3 to 7% of the world's  population. So we're a small- >> Yeah... >> bit of the population, yes. >> Yeah. In some wide boundary sense,  and this might offend some people,   but in some ways we're all indigenous,  right, to this earth, and we're captured   by this certain economic system and being  rushed along by the river that we're part of. But a, a part of us is indigenous, yes? >> Yes and no. Yes, every human  being is indigenous to the world.   And if you go back far enough in every single  person's ancestry, you're going to find people   who once lived very much in touch with  the earth. However, as of right now,   the term indigenous has a very specific  meaning, and it deals with the communities   that lived and were in touch with the people,  had their own systems, their own governments,   and then some type of colonial force came in and  caused havoc and destruction on the community. So right now it's a term of art.  So when I'm speaking about it,   I'm speaking specifically about the  modern definition of what it is to be   an indigenous person. And I think we do want  to be careful to not broaden the definition so   much that we forget the peoples that  it's meant to respond to. But also,   I do want people to remember that at their  heart, everyone is indigenous to this planet. Yeah. >> Thank you. That was clarifying. So  tell me more about the work. What are   you trying to accomplish with the Ishkode, uh,  F- Fund and, and your future work? And what's,   what's the big ask? What's, what's the,  the need and what's the opportunity? >> Well, as you mentioned, a very small  percentage of money goes to indigenous-led work. Yet so many of the indigenous communities  hold answers to many of the problems   we're facing today, to environmental  issues, to food security questions,   to how do you care for your elders and  your children? And I would like to see   a change in the amount of money going out.  And yes, I already mentioned that we're a   small percentage of the earth's population, but I  think we're holding much bigger answers than that. I would like to see an increase of  funding to indigenous communities,   not only to repair the things that happened in  the past, though I do think that is a part of it,   and when people learn the context and they  understand why things are the way they are   in our communities, I think they would agree  that there's some harm to be repaired and fixed. But I also genuinely believe that our  communities are poised at this moment in   time with everything that is happening around  us to be major players in the things that are   to come and in finding the solutions to the  things that we are facing as a world. This is   not a romanticization of the past. This is not  expecting people to-- I'm not trying to say to   you we're better or superior in any way, but  I do think that there are big missing pieces   in the solutions that are being created,  and I think we can play an important role. So I would absolutely love to see more  philanthropic dollars starting to be unlocked and   to flow into community, and I would like to see a  way of taking these philanthropic dollars, making   them more a part of a, a, a big capital stack,  if you will, and starting to solve some of the   issues that we have at this moment in time while  money still has the value that it has. Right? Because we know that there are changes  coming, and see what comes of it,   and h- see if we can exponentially speed  up the rate of finding some solutions. >> So what are some of the solutions  that indigenous, uh, communities could,   if we listened and there was support, um,  help the broader trajectory ahead of us? >> Well, we're in the middle of Climate  Week right now, so we're talking a lot   about climate. I genuinely believe the people who  have stewarded the lands understand the lands in   a very unique way. I was with a Zuni elder who  was talking about a drought that hit their area,   and they had this particular  watering area, and it dried up. And everyone was thinking, "What  are we gonna do? How are we gonna,   how are we gonna deal with our crops?" And he  remembered the name, a place name of a location,   and the word for water was in that  place name. And he said, "You know,   we've never had water there before, but  our ancestors must have known something." They went, they went to dig it up, and  there was water, enough water to be able   to feed the crops and keep them hydrated  and, and, um, irrigated throughout. And   that's just a tiny example. Built in our  languages, built in our stories, built in   our traditions are s- are stories of times when  there have been other types of climate collapses,   when there's been other shifting of temperatures,  and how did our community survive that? But not only that, there are governmental systems  forms that could help us as we are dealing with   geopolitical collapse all over the world. There  are stories of indigenous midwives and birth   workers who are bringing back traditional ways.  I mean, we have, especially in the United States,   incredibly high rates of maternal and  infant deaths, and people think, "Oh,   we have such an incredible, uh, medical system,"  yet we have high rates, high for the world. And these indigenous birth workers and midwives  are stepping up and giving us ideas because we   truly believe the way someone is born into this  world matters. And we also have death ways,   ways of, of birthing someone out of this life into  death. We're so scared of death in this world,   and there are so many teachings that can assist  us with that, and the list can go on and on. If there's anything that someone is interested  in, I guarantee that in some indigenous culture,   and probably more than one, there is  a clue, a way that maybe we can take   some of the things that we're missing  in modernity and improve upon them. >> What about reciprocity? That's  a, a core theme of the podcast,   as we're gonna need more of that going forward. How is reciprocity central to kind of indigenous  practices and, and communities, and we need to   learn and have a pathway forward. Um, could...  Is there some seed there that could grow? >> I'll speak about reciprocity, but I also  wanna fine-tune it to reciprocity and giving,   which is that growing up I was taught  a lot about every time you give,   something is going to come back to you. I remember at one point my grandfather  was talking to me about, about giving,   and it was embedded inside of me that  when you're going to give someone a gift,   you don't give any old thing, something  that's not that big of a deal to you. If   you're gonna give, you wanna give the  best, the best thing that you have. It should actually sting a little bit to  give that thing away, because otherwise   you don't ins- instinctively inside of  yourself understand the power of giving. >> And now our culture is  the exact opposite of that. >> Yeah. Yeah. But there's... The thing is  that if it stings a little bit and you are   giving something that really, really matters  to you, you're not going to forget that moment. And even if the person who receives it doesn't  understand the depth of what it is that you gave,   you do, and it changes you inside.  It helps reduce your connection to   things. You become less likely to hoard  and want to hold onto something. You're   less attached to objects because you  are always willing to give it away. >> The only time I've ever felt what  you just described is when I loved   someone and did something or gave them something. >> Yeah. >> And yeah. >> Can you imagine how much we would love others  if we did that with everyone we gave something to? >> And is this, like, a certain tribe or is  this- No... uh, ubiquitous in, in these cultures? >> Even though we are not related,  it is a theme I have found in every   indigenous culture I've ever been in.  It's hard because so many people wanna   talk about this general indigenous  culture as if there is one. There   is not one. Right. But I do find similar  ideas, similar values all the way across. >> I've been thinking a lot about this lately,  and you watch some of my podcasts and my Franklys,   and I'm really distinguishing between humans  and humanity, which is large numbers of humans,   especially with institutional  structures and hierarchy and surplus. And the reason that a lot of indigenous  communities around the world express these values,   which I think are aligned with our crucible of  where we came from is 'cause they're smaller   populations and numbers, and they're not in  this entire capitalist, uh, uh, you know,   I don't often say that, but this  superorganism structure in the world. So I just wonder how much of these values  and expressions of reciprocity and giving   are a product of smaller numbers  and actually less physical surplus. >> Mm-hmm. I, I don't know that that's it. >> Hmm. >> I think it has much more to do with the values  and the society in which you're living. I had the   opportunity to live in Poland from 1998 to 2000,  and I can remember this woman, for some reason she   took a liking to my little family, and she decided  that she wanted to have us over for a meal. And we were expats. We were living, you know,  with the ex- the surplus that you're given on   an expat contract. We had a beautiful home.  When we went into this woman's apartment,   it was this tiny little hallway  with a little water closet. Her   living room was also her and her  daughter's bedroom, a tiny kitchen. She served us this gorgeous eight-course meal.  I don't even know how much of her salary it must   have cost her to feed us that way, but it was  such a heartfelt gift. She was living in Warsaw,   Poland. It wasn't a small little community,  but I believe that some of the things that   have happened that have taken these values  away in Western culture hadn't hit there yet. They were still, they were still in  an older way of being and thinking   and doing. That was the same level of  reciprocity that we're speaking about. >> I hear and feel what you're saying because  I've personally softened in the last five years,   and I'm uber-focused on all the  crisis risks and what I see ahead. And, um, that focus has kept me away from  these human stories and our potential,   and I'm just seeing it in a lot more places, or  at least seeing the possibility of it. So I, I,   I have more hope than I used to despite, despite  what's coming. Let me ask you this, kind of,   um, and, and, uh, this, this is awkward  coming from a old privileged white guy. Um- But we talk about racism and  some of the other demographic,   uh, challenges in the world. Will  there always be a remorse and anger   of what happened in the genocide when white  people came to North America and everything   that happened? Um, or c- is it possible  that indigenous people, local farmers,   other people in Minnesota can work together  in coming decades to make a better future? Or is, is the, is the, is the trauma and the,   and the hurt too deep? Like, just an  honest question. I, I have no idea. >> I think that repair is awfully hard to get to   when there's so many people who don't  want to face that it even happened. >> Uh-huh. >> Or so many people who still wanna say,  "Well, it wasn't me, so why are you upset?" To just honestly hear the story and understand  the context of what happened can make all the   difference. I can only speak for myself.  I have no, no ability to speak for the   community at large. Everyone individually  is going to be unique in their answer.   But there are too many people who still wanna  pretend it didn't happen, or who minimize it,   or who come into our communities and say,  "But you've been given all these other things. Why haven't you improved yourself?" Without truly  understanding the context of the experience.   My own grandfather was taken forcibly from  our reservation, put into a boarding school,   and made to feel ashamed of himself,  and that has had a generational impact.   It impacted my mother and the way that she  raised me, and it impacted my life deeply. It's not ancient history. Until we can actually  have an honest conversation, we don't expect   everyone to come up and, and go overboard on  it, but could we at least just admit that it   happened, and that there's a reason for certain  circumstances that we're still living in today?   At the same time, there are a lot of indigenous  groups in the US and other places who are saying,   "Maybe we're never gonna get that,  but we need to do things right now,   and we are willing to make alliances  with people and start working together." There's a lot of work happening with native  and non-native peoples in the United States,   and they're willing to overlook that in  many cases. And I do think that sometimes,   sometimes it requires the  alliance to happen first,   and then the understanding comes. A lot of people  want to identify our communities by trauma,   and there is trauma, and it's a real  part of our family and our story. But we're so much more than our trauma, and  when people only wanna see us through the   lens of trauma and the lens of poverty,  they always miss the gifts that we have   to give. So we somehow have to figure out  a balance of yes, there's a context and   we should name it and we should own it,  and also this community is so much more. >> So flipping the relationship  between funder and, and, uh, recipient,   what will philanthropists, humans generally,  uh, opening their hearts to Ishkode and,   and others who are working in this space,  what are, what are the... Flipping it,   what are the gifts that we can receive from  indigenous communities? What can we learn? What can we experience  building on what you just said? >> Well, first of all, I want to  take that term of reciprocity,   which we talked about earlier, and speak about  it in the sort of, uh, philanthropic sense,   which is a lot of times people  look at philanthropy as charity,   as we have and you do not have, and we're  gonna come in and we're gonna help you. And if you come in in a rec-reciprocity mindset,  what you're going to say is, "We have something   that you need right now that we need to flow to  you to unlock the things that you have to offer,   and in exchange, we are going to receive  incredible things. You are going to bring   to us this understanding of how to deal with  the rivers, and what did you once know about   how to bring things back into balance, and you're  going to start assisting us in our own remembering   path to what it once meant when our ancestors  lived with the Earth in a particular way." Uh, we've mentioned already there are government  forms, there are ways you care for your elders,   there are ways of giving and exchanging  that could be learned. I mean, I could   give you stories and examples of things  that are already happening. Um, we have   indigenous elders. We have an indigenous elder  in Cordova, Alaska, who told me a few years ago,   "The salmon are not going to be at the Copper  River for maybe five to eight more years." And everyone around him said there's absolutely  no way. This year, for the first time in his   lifetime, three of the five species of salmon did  not return to the Copper River. It's happening.   And he knows that there's only so much that  can be done to restore that habitat. There's   on-only so many trees that can be planted to  try to bring the temperatures and the balance   of the ecosystem around the rivers back into  balance so that the salmon can come back again. So in the meantime, he is looking for other  solutions. He's planting kelp. He's saying,   "All right, do you-- We used to eat kelp, kelp all  the time. We have to have something to bridge what   we're losing with what we hope to repair one day,  and there's a, there's a gap there. But we have   some ideas, and if we look back and we think  about those old ways that we once did things,   I think we can come up with some solutions to  help us as we're in this in-between time when   some things are dying, and it's going  to take a while for them to regenerate. What else can we do to help  humanity survive this collapse?" >> I think we're kicking  out the rungs of the ladder,   um, behind us as we, or below us as we climb.  And I just, I think a lot of people have this,   uh, assumption that when things, when  there's disruption, we're just gonna go   back 50 years or whatever. I just  don't think there's going back. But I'm wondering if going forward there's  a possibility for ecologists and indigenous   leaders and communities and some form of  technology all together to create some new   way of regenerating living systems. And there's  a lot of talk this week at Climate Week about,   uh, regenerative agriculture and living systems  and how humans need to be regenerators instead of,   uh, extractors, those sorts of things. How can we   possibly do that without listening and  learning from indigenous communities? Like, what is the logic there? Do you agree? >> I don't think there is a logic to say we  can do it without the indigenous peoples. I   think actually our communities excel in that.  It's a constant thing. We are right now people   who have survived an entire societal  breakdown ourselves, not created by us,   but be created by others who came in and wiped out  culture and language and ways of living and family   and in community, and we said, "All right, so how  do we restore ourselves in the modern context?" We are constantly having to figure out  how to rebalance and to reclaim the things   that have been lost, and I think we're in a  perfect position to assist with doing that. >> So how are some of the differences,  um, between the way that, um, uh,   Western organizations and structures do  stewardship and indigenous communities? Have you noticed differences? >> Well, if we go to the original, um,  environmental movements, for example,   a lot of the tenets are we need to conserve  the environment from humans. So it's the idea   that we have to keep humans out of it.  We have to have these protected areas.   Humans shouldn't do something, and  that's the best thing for the Earth. But when you talk to indigenous peoples, that's  completely different. Humans are a part of the   environment. Without humans doing their job  stewarding the lands, stewarding the plants and   the animals in a positive way, you're not going  to have as thriving of a community. I have another   example for you. I was in Hawaii, and I was on  a taro farm, and they were restoring the lands,   and they were trying to get rid of invasive  plants, invasive grasses and trees and things   that had overgrown into the area that were  brought in by people from the outside. And one day, as they'd been doing all this work on  their land, this bird showed up on the property,   and they recognize it, and it's  a very sacred bird to the native   Hawaiians. It's also highly endangered.  Now, when you see one of these birds,   you're supposed to report it to the government  agencies and say, "This en- this endangered bird." So they came out, and they said, "Oh yeah, you  have a couple of these birds on your property.   Well, you have to stop all work now. You can't  do any work because you could disrupt the birds."   But what they forgot was that these  birds lay their eggs in nests on the   ground. The invasive grasses that they were  pulling out were the very reason that these   birds were so endangered because they were  going in and, um, choking out the nests. So if they stopped pulling the invasive  grasses, the birds wouldn't be able to   thrive on this property. So finally, and you  know, we don't want to get anyone in trouble,   but they finally had to just say, "You know,  we don't, we don't wanna know what's going on,   but we want these birds to thrive."  And the last time I spoke with them,   of the 400 of these birds still in existence,  40 of them were spotted on this area of land. It was well-intentioned to say if you  find this endangered animal, this bird,   you should stop your work, but yet the  stewardship of the human pulling these   invasive things out of the earth so that the earth  could thrive as it was intended in that particular   ecosystem was the exact answer that was needed  to bring this bird back from endangered status. >> What's the challenge here with your  work? I believe you fund 200 different, uh,   communities or NGOs that are all indigenous, and  you-- there's thousands more that need funding,   so you have to raise large dollars to  be able to support these people. What   is the challenge for you trying  to grow this fund and this, this,   uh, movement towards getting more money  flowing towards indigenous communities and the,   the things that we get in return for that  as seeds for different cultural responses? >> I think there are numerous. I find it  fascinating in the philanthropic world   that people are so risk-averse. When you  talk to people in their venture capital,   they are willing to put millions of dollars  on big risks that may or may not ever pay off,   and in the investment world,  that makes sense to them. Yet they-- that risk tolerance doesn't  translate into philanthropic giving.   Why are we not more open to saying  we're going to take a chance? You put   these little nonprofits through greater  due diligence and proofs than they put   these massive investment opportunities,  and I think that's really interesting. And I'm not saying there has never been  a project that didn't succeed. Of course   there has. But I find it so interesting that  if there is an indigenous project that fails,   it's used as, "Oh, see, this is why we don't fund  indigenous peoples." It happens all the time in   non-indigenous 501(c)(3)s, and nobody says, "Well,  that's-- we should just not fund any 501(c)(3)s." We're held to a different standard,   and I think that's interesting. I think we  as a community should pause and ask ourselves   why. Why do we put a higher level of  requirement on indigenous peoples? >> I'm not an expert at all in, in this, um,   but it seems pretty obvious to me that there  are peoples in our country, in our continent,   that have already lived through a version of The  Great Simplification, and why shouldn't we be   looking to them and listening for some answers and  some direction and some just ways of discourse? What about governance and things like that?  What can we learn, uh, um, along those lines? >> Well, one of the things that I learned  early on is, in our community at least,   is that the greatest leader is not the person  who is standing on the top looking down and   barking down orders. The leader at their  heart, the Ogichidaa, is the one who goes   underneath the community and lifts them up  on their shoulders, that helps them rise. And I think just that sense of what it  is to be a leader from that perspective   can shift so much. People c- talk about  servant leadership. I think it is that,   but maybe slightly tweaked. That's one piece. >> That's not just one tribe. You've  seen that- Yeah... like across the board? >> Absolutely. That concept that the leader  has a responsibility to the community,   not just this ability or this authority  to bark things out and say, "Well,   I have this idea and let's take it from here." I think that's very powerful, especially  at a time where we need to be inspiring   the creativity of everyone. I believe that  anyone on Earth right now was born for this   time and has something innate within them that  can help us all survive the things that are   coming. That's why we are here, and a great  leader is going to inspire that to come out,   is going to inspire people  to tap deep inside and say,   "What is that thing that I have to offer the  world at this unique moment that we're in?" I also have noticed justice systems.  I'm an attorney. I have seen state court   judges come to Indigenous peacemakers and  say, "Help me understand this because our   justice sysm- system isn't working the way that  we were hoping it could work." There are so many   pieces of governance. The Haudenosaunee  are starting to write books saying,   "We had some- something to do with  this United States Constitution. There were things learned from  us, but you didn't take it all,   and there are pieces missing, and not  having those pieces has impacted its   effectiveness. We're standing here ready to  share the rest if you're open to hearing it." >> Can you share one of those pieces  that's missing, something along the lines? >> Well, one of the things that they were  missing was the leadership of women. Uh,   whenever, and this is another thing I've noticed  everywhere I've ever gone when there has been a   s- a series of colonizers moving into places, one  of the very first things they did is they removed   women from leadership. And when I say that,  there's people who will have a visceral reaction. "Are you saying women are better than  men?" No. I'm saying that women have   a very unique role in leadership, as do  men, and you need the combination of the   strengths of each in order to move forward in  a very collective way. But when they came in,   they knocked down the women who had a  particular role in their communities and said,   "Only the men can speak," and they  threw everything out of balance. But that's just one piece.  There's a lot more to it. >> So we, just to be clear, the US Constitution  was based on input from Haudenosa- Haudenosaun- >> Haudenosaunee... >> Haudenosaunee people, but we  picked and chose the things that   we included- Yes... and we left  out some- Yes... some doozies. >> And there's a lot more,   and I'm not Haudenosaunee and I  don't feel qualified to speak to it. >> Yeah. >> But there's a book that  was just published where,   where different Haudenosaunee elders came  in and brought in different pieces and said,   "You didn't bring in this. You didn't bring  in this." And when you have a beautiful system   and you take out some key pieces, it's not ever  going to be as effective as it could have been. I think we've done some amazing things  in the United States. I'm not trying to   negate everything that has ever happened.  But we are now watching this collapse of   our governmental systems. transcript_segments.text: >> If we go to the original environmental  movements, a lot of the tenets are,
we have to keep humans out of it. We  have to have these protected areas. But
when you talk to indigenous peoples, that's  completely different. Humans are a part of
the environment. Without humans doing their job,  stewarding the lands, stewarding the plants and
the animals in a positive way, you're not  going to have as thriving of a community.
>> Today I'm pleased to be joined by my friend  Victoria Sweet, who is the founder of the Ishkode
Fund. Uh, today we will explore how indigenous  ideas can help address our hardest challenges,
and how Victoria, uh, enables critical  funding to reach indigenous-led groups.
Uh, Victoria Sweet is an immediate descendant of
the White Earth Nation and granddaughter  of a native boarding school survivor.
Through the Ishkode Fund, Victoria works to  restore balance between people and the Earth,
as well as provide support that will help  strengthen the fire of indigenous leadership
and innovation that has long sustained native  communities. She has worked at the National
Council of Juvenile and Family Court Judges,  where she trained state and tribal judges hearing
domestic violence and human trafficking  cases involving native community members.
She also worked with the Whitener Group  supporting tribal justice systems in Alaska, and
as the director of the di- indigenous communities  portfolio of grantees during her time at the NoVo
Foundation. In our conversation, Victoria explains  that donating to indigenous-led causes is not a
matter of charity, but instead an investment and  reciprocal relationship from which we all benefit.
She shares specific examples of  how indigenous communities share
knowledge that benefits everyone nearby, despite  indigenous-led organizations receiving only one
quarter of 1% of philanthropic dollars in the  United States. Beyond philanthropy, though,
uh, Victoria challenges each of us  to get to know a local indigenous
community and be open to the possibility  of learning something new and unexpected.
With that, please welcome Victoria Sweet.
Victoria Sweet, great to see you.  Welcome to The Great Simplification.
>> Thanks, Nate.
>> So you are the founder and CEO of the  Ishkode Foundation, and you are of direct
ancestry with the White Earth Nation, which  I believe is Ojibwe. And you've spent most of
your career strengthening systems to protect  indigenous people, including justice reform,
tribal court development, um, and  now community-led philanthropy.
Uh, maybe you could start by saying  what the word Ishkode means and why
that was central to your work and your,  your trajectory that brought you here.
>> Thanks. Yes. The Ishkode is actually a word in  the Anishinaabe language, and a lot of indigenous
languages are not noun-based languages, so  they don't translate exactly into English.

fire. It's fire as medicine. It's fire  as transformation. It's the fire that
exists in every single person when you feel  something inside of you, like a spark, an idea,
a knowing about something. And in our tradition,  a name is so much more than just a name.

So when this fund was originated, it made a lot  of sense to me that we needed to name it first
because that gave it some direction, some  guidance. How can we take a fund that's all
about flowing money and turn it into some kind  of healing fire, some kind of transformation?
And then when you have this  transformative fire and you
look at the world with the fires  that are burning down and all of
the damage and destruction that has been  done, you have unhealthy, harmful fire,
and then you have its opposite. And I'd really  love to see this fund represent the opposite.
>> So I wanna get to your fund, um, in  a moment and the work that you're doing.
But two, uh, um, pre-questions. What do you  think the role of philanthropy is generally
in the meta-crisis world and facing all the  things that we're facing? And then a subset of
that is my understanding is a very tiny percent  of philanthropy is directed towards indigenous,
uh, populations, and you're  trying to increase that.
So maybe you could set the, the stage for  that. Um, why is this work so important now?
>> Philanthropy can play a very interesting  role. Uh, it's philanthropic d- um,
donated charitable dollars. So oftentimes  you can use philanthropy for things that
investments and other types of capital  won't do. It can seed fund something
where an investor says, "Well, we have to  have certain, uh, guarantees to back it."

stack. Philanthropy can go in and buoy up. So for  instance, we fund a lot of nonprofits. For me,

and we don't think it's going to  happen through these other ways.

I think a lot of people don't  understand the power of what it

and then we'll help these native peoples,  these indigenous peoples." And they haven't
had a chance to actually see the beauty  of what these communities have to offer.

>> Yeah. In some wide boundary sense,  and this might offend some people,
